title: Two Principles for Normalizing Struggle in a Given Classroom
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Drawing on a professional-development session with secondary teachers in Cache County, Utah, Stuart lays out two research-grounded principles for making struggle a normal, motivating part of a classroom rather than a source of shame. His first principle holds that struggle must be universal within a class; if only some students visibly struggle, those students will read their difficulty as evidence they don't belong, triggering what he calls the Anti-Belonging Hamster Wheel Effect. This requires teachers to set uniformly high expectations for all students rather than differentiating expectations downward. His second principle is that struggle must reliably lead to growth: effort sustained without any sense of payoff is unsustainable, so teachers must explicitly teach sub-skills, define success as movement toward a high bar, and frame that bar as bigger than the teacher-student relationship itself. Together the two principles describe the mechanics by which a struggle-is-normal classroom culture is built and sustained.
points: Struggle only reads as "normal" to a student if virtually everyone in the room visibly struggles; uneven struggle produces a Belonging problem, not just an Effort problem.
Stuart names the "Anti-Belonging Hamster Wheel Effect," the phenomenon of students who feel uniquely challenged spending cognitive energy scanning for social-exclusion signals instead of learning.
High expectations alone are insufficient; teachers must explicitly teach the sub-skills and prior knowledge that make reaching those expectations possible.
Framing success as growth toward a bar bigger than the teacher's own preferences, rather than compliance to please the teacher, sustains effort over the long term.
quotes: In one of the sessions, we were looking at the mechanics of creating secondary classrooms in which struggle is normal and — dare we hope for it? — even desirable for all students.

If struggle is something that many kids in a class do not normally experience, then, definitionally, struggle is not normal in that classroom. As a result, in such places the students who do struggle will tend toward demotivation due to an awareness that they don't Belong.
And so the "struggle is normal" classroom has to be one in which the bar is set very high. This doesn't mean that you only need high expectations to help students grow.

Struggle alone, however, does not motivation make. No human being can struggle in futility indefinitely. If a person is to persist in effort over the long term, that person must gain a sense, amidst the strain, that the effort is paying off in some way.

Teach, model, and reinforce the sub-skills and prior knowledge bits that make growth toward your high expectations possible. As the teacher, define success relentlessly as growth toward the high bar you've set.
